nameStory: The name 'fragilis' comes from Latin meaning 'fragile' or 'delicate,' perfectly describing this tiny sea slug's soft, translucent body that can be easily damaged by rough handling or wave action. Like all nudibranchs (pronounced NEW-dih-branks), it breathes through exposed gills, which is what 'nudibranch' means - 'naked gills' in Latin.
description: Doto fragilis is a tiny sea slug, or nudibranch, that crawls along underwater surfaces in New England's coastal waters. These soft-bodied marine creatures are related to snails but have lost their shells through evolution. They're typically very small, often less than an inch long, with translucent bodies and finger-like projections called cerata that help them breathe and digest food. This particular species is extremely rare in New England waters, with only one confirmed sighting recorded.

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Soft, translucent body that feels gelatinous to the touch, like a tiny piece of clear jelly that can compress easily under gentle pressure

idTips.label: Cerata arrangement
idTips.description: Multiple finger-like projections along the back that may have club-shaped tips, feeling smooth and slightly sticky when gently touched

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically less than an inch long, easily fitting on your thumbnail with room to spare

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides slowly and smoothly across surfaces using its muscular foot, leaving no visible trail but moving with a rhythmic wave-like motion

idTips.label: Head region
idTips.description: Two small tentacle-like structures called rhinophores at the front that help it smell and taste the water

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, typically crawling on hydroids (tiny colonial animals) which they feed upon. Look for them in tide pools, on pier pilings, or attached to seaweed in areas with good water circulation. They prefer protected areas where wave action won't damage their delicate bodies.

seasonality.spring: May become more active as water temperatures rise, making them slightly easier to spot during low tide explorations.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation when warm water temperatures make them most active and visible in tide pools and shallow areas.
seasonality.fall: Still present but activity may decrease as water temperatures begin to cool, requiring more careful searching.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed due to cold water temperatures and reduced activity, plus harsh weather makes tide pool exploration difficult.

funFact: Nudibranchs like Doto fragilis are often called the 'butterflies of the sea' because many species display incredibly vibrant colors and intricate patterns, and some can even steal stinging cells from their prey and use them for their own defense!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny sea slugs or even small anemones when not moving, but the distinctive gliding motion and finger-like cerata help distinguish it. Remember: if it's sliding smoothly across a surface, it's likely a nudibranch; if it's staying put and waving in the current, it's probably an anemone.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England (only one recorded observation) means any sighting would be scientifically significant and worth reporting to local marine biology organizations or iNaturalist for expert verification.
compareHints: Doto fragilis differs from its relative the Crowned Seaslug (Doto coronata) primarily in the shape and arrangement of its cerata - the finger-like projections on its back. While both are tiny and translucent, each Doto species has a unique 'fingerprint' pattern of these projections that helps scientists tell them apart under magnification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Doto species found in New England, the Crowned Seaslug is the most commonly encountered and serves as the 'type species' - essentially the gold standard that defines what a Doto should look like.
Compared to its relative the Crowned Seaslug (Doto coronata), Doto formosa tends to be more translucent and delicate-looking with less pronounced cerata tips.
